source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2
note: Verses 16-17 are missing from the source text (jumps from v15 to v18).

verses.translation: And another time{H6471} Yeshua{H3442} began to teach{H3925} at the shore{H2348} of the sea{H3220}, and a great{H7227} people{H5971} assembled{H622}. Therefore he went up{H5927} into a small{H6996} boat and sat{H3427} in the sea{H3220}, and all{H3605} the company{H2428} sat{H3427} at the lip{H8193} of the sea{H3220}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses החיל (ha-chayil — 'the company/host', H2428) for the crowd. Greek ὄχλος ('crowd') is civilian. The Hebrew uses the military/organizational term for an assembled force — the same word for an army division or productive capacity (Ruth 4:11, 1 Sam 10:26). The audience is framed as an assembled host, not a random crowd.

Uses בשפת הים ('at the lip of the sea', H8193+H3220) — the OT idiom for the seashore (Gen 22:17, 41:3; Ex 2:3, 14:30; Josh 11:4; 1 Kgs 4:29). Greek παρὰ τὴν θάλασσαν ('beside the sea') is generic. The 'lip' metaphor personifies the sea — it has a mouth edge — which is a Semitic idiom absent from Greek.
translation_notes: 'Lip' for sfat — preserving the Hebrew body-metaphor for the shoreline.

verses.translation: And he was proclaiming{H1875} to them and disciplining{H3256} them with many{H7227} parables{H4912}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מייסרם (meyasrem — 'disciplining them', H3256, from יסר — 'to discipline/chastise/instruct'). Greek ἐδίδασκεν ('was teaching') is neutral. The Hebrew verb יסר is the Proverbs discipline verb (Prov 9:7, 19:18, 29:17,19) — teaching through correction and moral formation. A back-translator from Greek would use מלמד ('teaching'), not מייסר ('disciplining').

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: A man{H120} went out{H3318} to sow{H2232} his seed{H2233}.
And while he sowed{H2232}, some grains{H1715} fell{H5307} near{H7138} the way{H1870}, and birds{H5775} came{H935} and ate{H398} them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גרעינים (garginim — 'grains/kernels', H1715) — a specific word for individual seed kernels. Greek simply uses the implied subject from σπείρειν ('to sow'). The Hebrew specifies the physical form of the seed.

verses.translation: And others fell{H5307} in a place{H4725} of stones{H68} where there was not much{H7227} earth{H6083}, and immediately it came out{H3318}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עפר (afar — 'earth/dust', H6083) — the Genesis creation word (Gen 2:7 — man formed from afar). Greek γῆ ('earth/soil') is generic. The Hebrew uses the specific dust-of-creation word, giving the thin soil a Genesis resonance.

verses.translation: And it withered{H3001} when the sun{H8121} struck{H5221} it, for it had no root{H8328}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הכהו (hikahu — 'struck it', H5221, from נכה — 'to strike/smite') — the OT verb for God striking enemies (Ex 3:20, 7:17,20; 12:12,29). The sun 'smites' the plant like a divine blow. Greek ἐκαυματίσθη ('was scorched') is meteorological. The Hebrew personalizes the sun as an active smiter.

verses.translation: And another fell{H5307} among{H996} the thorns{H6975}, and the thorns{H6975} grew{H1431} together and choked{H2614} it, and it did not give{H5414} fruit{H6529}.
And another fell{H5307} in the good{H2896} earth{H776}, and it bore — one thirty{H7970} and one sixty{H8346} and one a hundred{H3967}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בטוב הארץ ('in the good of the earth') — 'the good of the land' echoes Genesis 45:18,20 where Pharaoh tells Joseph's family to eat 'the good of the land' (טוב ארץ מצרים). Greek εἰς τὴν γῆν τὴν καλήν ('into the good earth'). The Hebrew construct is a partitive — 'the goodness that belongs to the earth' — while the Greek is adjectival.
translation_notes: Numbers are abbreviated in the source text: ל'=30, ס'=60, ק'=100.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559}: Whoever has ears{H241}, let him hear{H8085}.

textual_notes: Echoes Deuteronomy 29:3 and Ezekiel 12:2 — the refrain about having ears but not hearing.

verses.translation: And when they were aside, the students{H8527} asked{H7592} him about the parable{H4912}.
And he said{H559}: To you it is given{H5414} to understand{H995} the secrets{H5475} of the kingdom{H4467} of heaven{H8064}, but to them not — except in similitudes.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses סודות (sodot — 'secrets/counsels', H5475, from סוד — 'council/secret') — the OT word for being admitted to God's inner council (Amos 3:7: 'He reveals His secret — סוד — to His servants the prophets'; Ps 25:14; Job 15:8; Jer 23:18). Greek μυστήριον ('mystery') is a Hellenistic religious term for initiation secrets. The Hebrew concept is prophetic — admission to the divine council; the Greek concept is cultic — initiation mystery. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as מוסטריון, not use the prophetic סוד.
Uses מלכות שממיי ('kingdom of heaven') — again the Jewish circumlocution, consistent with 1:15 and this chapter's v.26,30. Greek consistently has 'kingdom of God.'

Uses דמיונות (dimyonot — 'similitudes/likenesses', from H1819 דמה — 'to be like') — a different word from משלים ('parables', used in v.2). The outsiders receive dimyonot (visual likenesses); the insiders receive understanding. Greek uses παραβολαῖς for both.
translation_notes: 'Secrets' for sodot — preserving the prophetic divine-council concept.
textual_notes: Amos 3:7: 'Surely the Lord YHWH does nothing without revealing His secret (סוֹדוֹ) to His servants the prophets.' The students are admitted to the prophetic סוד.

verses.translation: So that they may see{H7200} yet not see{H7200}, and hear{H8085} yet not hear{H8085} — understanding{H995} in their sins{H2403} that they are atoned for{H3722}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The Hebrew ending is בחטאתיהם שהם מכופרים ('in their sins that they are atoned for') — a positive statement that sins are atoned. Greek ends with μήποτε ἐπιστρέψωσιν καὶ ἀφεθῇ αὐτοῖς ('lest they turn and be forgiven') — a negative statement implying prevention of forgiveness. These are opposite conclusions. The Hebrew says the parables lead to understanding that sins are atoned; the Greek says the parables prevent understanding and forgiveness. Irreconcilable difference.
Again uses מכופרים (mechupparim — 'atoned for', H3722) — the consistent Yom Kippur vocabulary.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew ending: 'understanding that their sins are atoned for' (positive). Greek ending: 'lest they turn and be forgiven' (negative prevention). Opposite theological conclusions.
textual_notes: The Isaiah source (Isa 6:9-10) in the MT also has a complex structure. The Hebrew Gospel appears to resolve the apparent cruelty of the Isaiah quotation by affirming atonement.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: Do you not understand{H995} this similitude{H1823}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses דמיון (dimyon — 'similitude/likeness', H1823) — different from both משל (mashal — 'proverb/parable', v.2) and the plural דמיונות (v.11). The Hebrew has multiple words for parabolic speech; Greek uses παραβολή throughout.

verses.translation: The one who sows{H2232} is the one who proclaims{H1875} the word{H1697}.
That which fell{H5307} on the way{H1870} — they are those who hear{H8085} the words{H1697} of God{H410}, and immediately the Adversary{H7854} comes{H935} and removes it from their heart{H3820}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלבם ('from their heart', H3820) — the Adversary removes the word from the heart (the seat of understanding in Hebrew thought). Greek αἴρει τὸν λόγον τὸν ἐσπαρμένον εἰς αὐτούς ('takes away the word sown in them') — 'in them,' not specifically 'in their heart.' The Hebrew locates the spiritual battleground in the lev (heart).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the words of God' (דברי האל). Greek: τὸν λόγον ('the word'). Hebrew specifies the divine source.
textual_notes: Verses 16-17 are absent from this Hebrew source. The explanation of the rocky-ground seed appears to be missing.

verses.translation: And that which fell{H5307} in the land{H776} of thorns{H6975} — they are those who hear{H8085} the teachings{H1875}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הדרשות (ha-derashot — 'the teachings/expositions', from H1875 דרש — 'to seek/expound') — the Hebrew term for Torah exposition, the root of 'midrash.' Greek τὸν λόγον ('the word') is generic. The Hebrew frames what they hear as derashot — formal Torah teachings.

verses.translation: And the deficiencies of the world{H5769} and the loss{H6} of worldly riches{H6239} choke{H2614} them, and they remain without fruit{H6529}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חסרונות העולם ('deficiencies of the world') for what chokes. Greek αἱ μέριμναι τοῦ αἰῶνος ('the cares/anxieties of the age'). The Hebrew says it is the world's lacks — its emptiness and insufficiency — that choke; the Greek says it is worries. Different diagnosis: deprivation vs. anxiety.

Uses אובדן העושרים ('the loss/destruction of riches', H6 from אבד — 'to perish'). Greek ἡ ἀπάτη τοῦ πλούτου ('the deceit of wealth'). The Hebrew says riches are lost/destroyed; the Greek says riches deceive. Different moral: impermanence vs. deception.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'deficiencies of the world.' Greek: 'cares of the age.' Different source of choking.
Hebrew: 'loss of riches.' Greek: 'deceit of riches.' Different moral about wealth.

verses.translation: And that which fell{H5307} on the good{H2896} earth{H776} represents those who hear{H8085} and put into practice and make{H6213} good{H2896} fruit{H6529}, until from one{H259} grain come thirty{H7970}, and from one{H259} sixty{H8346}, and from one{H259} a hundred{H3967}. Whoever has ears{H241} to hear{H8085}, let him hear{H8085}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ומשימין בפועל ('and put into practice' — literally 'place into action'). Greek uses καρποφοροῦσιν ('they bear fruit'). The Hebrew adds an action component absent from Greek — not merely bearing fruit passively but actively practicing what was heard. This reflects the Jewish emphasis on deed over belief.
The 'ears to hear' refrain is repeated from v.9 — the Hebrew places it at the end of the parable explanation, where Greek does not. This frames the explanation itself as requiring ears to hear.

verses.translation: And he says{H559} to them: No man{H120} places{H5117} a burning{H1197} lamp{H5216} under the thorn-bush, nor under the bed{H4296}, but a man{H120} places it on the menorah{H4501}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses דרדור (dardur — 'thorn-bush') where Greek has μόδιον ('bushel basket/measuring vessel'). A thorn-bush and a measuring basket are completely different objects. No back-translator from Greek would produce 'thorn-bush.' The Hebrew may preserve a different version of the saying rooted in the agricultural Palestinian landscape.

Uses מנורה (menorah, H4501) — the specific Temple lampstand (Ex 25:31-40, 37:17-24). Greek λυχνία ('lampstand') is generic. The Hebrew evokes the Temple menorah — the light is placed on the sacred stand, not a common household fixture.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'thorn-bush' (דרדור). Greek: 'bushel basket' (μόδιον). Different object.
translation_notes: 'Menorah' for the lampstand — preserving the Temple connection.

verses.translation: No thing{H1697} is hidden{H5641} or concealed{H5956} that shall not be known{H5234}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses a pair of near-synonyms: נסתר (nistar — 'hidden', H5641) and נעלם (ne'elam — 'concealed', H5956). Hebrew poetry characteristically pairs synonyms for emphasis. Greek has κρυπτόν... ἀπόκρυφον ('hidden... secret') — a similar pair, but the Hebrew verbs carry distinct OT connotations: nistar is used for God's hidden things (Deut 29:28), ne'elam for sins hidden from view (Lev 4:13, 5:2-4).

verses.translation: Whoever has ears{H241} to hear{H8085}, let him hear{H8085}.
And he says{H559} to you: See{H7200} what you hear{H8085}, for with the measure{H4060} you measure{H4058}, with that you shall receive{H6901} — with increase.

one_way_hebrew: Uses באותה מדה שתמדדו באותה תקבלו ('with the measure you measure, with that you shall receive') — a Hebrew proverb known from the Mishnah (Sotah 1:7): במדה שאדם מודד בה מודדין לו ('with the measure a person measures, it is measured to him'). Greek ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖτε μετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν ('with what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you'). Both reflect this proverb, but the Hebrew adds בהגדלה ('with increase') — God gives back more than what was measured. This addition is absent from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'with increase' (בהגדלה). Greek adds καὶ προστεθήσεται ὑμῖν ('and more shall be added to you'). Similar concept but different phrasing.
textual_notes: Mishnah Sotah 1:7 contains the same proverb: 'With the measure a person measures, it is measured to him.'

verses.translation: And whoever has, it shall be given{H5414} to him; and whoever does not have — even that which he has shall be seized{H1497} from him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יגזלו (yigzelu — 'they shall seize/rob', H1497, from גזל), consistent with 2:20. The violent robbery verb. Greek ἀρθήσεται ('shall be taken away') is a gentle passive removal. The Hebrew says what little remains will be violently seized — robbery, not mere loss.

verses.translation: And he further said{H559} to them: Thus is the kingdom{H4467} of heaven{H8064} — like a man{H120} who sows{H2232} good{H2896} seed{H2233} in the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלכות שממיי ('kingdom of heaven') — the consistent Jewish circumlocution. Greek βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ('kingdom of God'). This is the fourth occurrence in Mark of this circumlocution (1:15, 4:11, 4:26, 4:30), consistently replacing Greek 'kingdom of God.'
Hebrew adds טוב ('good') to describe the seed. Greek has no qualifier — just σπόρον ('seed'). The Hebrew specifies the quality of the seed.

verses.translation: And he sleeps{H3462} day{H3117} and night{H3915} and rests{H5117}, and the seed{H2233} grows{H1431} and puts forth seed{H2232}, and he does not know{H3045}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ונח (ve-nach — 'and rests', H5117, from נוח — 'to rest') — the Shabbat/Noah rest verb. The sower rests while creation grows — an image of the creation Sabbath. Greek καθεύδῃ ('sleeps') is merely sleeping. The Hebrew adds theological rest — the sower participates in God's sabbatical pattern, resting while the earth does its work (Gen 2:2-3).

verses.translation: And moreover, the earth{H776} produces{H1431}: first{H7223} the grass{H6212}, and then the ears{H7641}, and then the wheat{H2406} fills{H4390} the ear{H7641}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שבולים (shibbolim — 'ears of grain', H7641) — the word from the Shibboleth episode (Judg 12:6), from Pharaoh's dream (Gen 41:5-7,22-27), and from the gleaning of Ruth (Ruth 2:2). Greek στάχυν ('ear of grain') is a direct equivalent. The Hebrew carries the full OT grain-narrative tradition.

verses.translation: And when the fruit{H6529} is complete{H7999}, immediately they put in the sickle{H4038}, for it is the time{H6256} of harvest{H7105}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נשלם (nishlam — 'is complete/made whole', H7999, from שלם — 'to be complete/at peace'). Greek παραδοῖ ('yields/hands over'). The Hebrew implies the fruit reaches שלמות (shlemut — completion/wholeness); the Greek implies the fruit surrenders itself. Different metaphor — maturity vs. yielding.
textual_notes: Joel 4:13 (Hebrew 3:13): שִׁלְחוּ מַגָּל כִּי בָשַׁל קָצִיר — 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.' The Hebrew Gospel echoes Joel's eschatological harvest imagery.

verses.translation: And he says{H559} to you: To what shall I compare{H1819} the kingdom{H4467} of the Name{H8034}? To what likeness{H1823} shall I liken{H1819} it?

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלכות השם ('the kingdom of the Name', H4467+H8034) — again using השם (HaShem) as the reverential circumlocution for YHWH. Greek βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ('kingdom of God'). Consistent with the Hebrew Gospel's pattern throughout Mark.

The double question אדמה...אדמהו echoes Isaiah 40:18: 'To whom then will you liken God? And what likeness (דמות) will you set alongside him?' and 40:25: 'To whom will you compare me (תדמיוני) that I should be equal?' The Hebrew frames Yeshua's parable introduction in the language of Isaiah's divine incomparability.
textual_notes: Isaiah 40:18: וְאֶל מִי תְּדַמְּיוּן אֵל — 'To whom will you liken God?' Same root דמה in the same rhetorical question pattern.

verses.translation: It is like a grain of mustard{H2623} — when it is sown{H2232} in the earth{H776}, it is smaller{H6996} than all{H3605} the seeds{H2233} that are in the earth{H776}.

And when it is sown{H2232}, it grows{H1431} and becomes greater{H1419} than all{H3605} the other herbs{H6212}, and makes many grains and branches{H6057}, so that the birds{H5775} of heaven{H8064} dwell{H7931} in the shade{H6738} of the branch{H6057}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עופות השמים דרים בצל הענף ('the birds of heaven dwell in the shade of the branch') — echoing Ezekiel 17:23: 'Under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches they shall dwell' (בצל דליותיו תשכנה). Also Daniel 4:12,21. Greek κατασκηνοῦν ὑπὸ τὴν σκιὰν αὐτοῦ ('nest under its shadow'). The Hebrew uses the Ezekiel/Daniel world-tree imagery — the kingdom as a cosmic tree sheltering the nations.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 17:23: 'On the mountain of the height of Israel I will plant it, and it will bear branches and produce fruit and become a noble cedar. Under it every bird of every wing shall dwell; in the shade of its branches they shall dwell.'

verses.translation: Many{H7227} such images{H8544} he said{H559} to them, so that they might understand{H995}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תמונות (temunot — 'images/forms', H8544) — the same word from the second commandment: 'You shall not make any image — תמונה' (Ex 20:4; Deut 4:12,15,16,23,25). Greek παραβολαῖς ('parables'). The Hebrew calls the parables 'images' — the same word prohibited for idolatrous representation. Yeshua creates verbal תמונות (images) of the kingdom. A back-translator from Greek would use משלים ('parables'), not the laden תמונות.

CRITICAL: Hebrew says the purpose is שיבינו ('so they might understand'). Greek says καθὼς ἠδύναντο ἀκούειν ('as they were able to hear'). Different purpose: Hebrew = to enable understanding; Greek = as much as they could receive. The Hebrew is optimistic about the parables' function.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'so they might understand.' Greek: 'as they were able to hear.' Different purpose.

verses.translation: And he did not speak{H1696} to them without images{H8544}, and therefore he explained them aside.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מבארו (meva'aro — 'explained them', H874, from באר — 'to explain/make clear'). This is the verb from Deuteronomy 1:5: 'Moshe began to explain (באר) this Torah.' Greek ἐπέλυεν ('solved/resolved'). The Hebrew frames Yeshua's private explanations using the same verb as Moses explaining Torah. A back-translator from Greek would use פתר ('interpreted') or פרש ('explained'), not the Mosaic באר.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 1:5: הוֹאִיל מֹשֶׁה בֵּאֵר אֶת הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת — 'Moshe began to explain this Torah.' Same verb באר.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them on that day{H3117}, when evening{H6153} came{H6213}: Let us cross over{H5674} to the other side.
And they released{H5117} the troops{H2428}, and he went up{H5927} into one{H259} small{H6996} boat, and they entered{H935} the sea{H3220} — other boats with him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses החיילות (ha-chaylot — 'the troops', H2428) for the crowd being dismissed. Greek τὸν ὄχλον ('the crowd'). Consistent with v.1 where the crowd is called חיל. The Hebrew consistently treats the audience as an assembled military-style host.

Uses הניחו (hinichu — 'they released/set down', H5117, from נוח — 'to rest') — they 'rested' the troops, i.e., dismissed them. Greek ἀφέντες ('leaving'). The Hebrew verb again uses the rest/shabbat root.

verses.translation: And then a great{H1419} and strong{H2389} wind{H7307} arose{H6965}, and waves{H1530}, until the boat began to fill{H4390}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רוח (ruach — 'wind/spirit', H7307) — the same word used throughout for 'the Holy Spirit.' The word's dual meaning creates a subtle tension: is this merely wind, or is it a spirit? Greek λαῖλαψ μεγάλη ἀνέμου ('a great windstorm') is unambiguous. The Hebrew ambiguity is natural to the language.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} was sleeping{H3462} in the stern{H3411} on a cushion{H3523}, and they woke{H6974} him and said{H559}: Rabbi, do you not turn{H6437} to us? For see{H7200} that we are perishing{H6}!

one_way_hebrew: Uses בירכתים (be-yarketayim — 'in the far recesses/stern', H3411) — echoing Jonah 1:5: 'Jonah had gone down into the recesses of the vessel (ירכתי הספינה) and had lain down and fallen fast asleep.' The verbal parallel is striking — both Yeshua and Jonah sleep in the yarketei ha-sefinah during a storm. The Hebrew Mark deliberately evokes the Jonah narrative. Greek ἐν τῇ πρύμνῃ ('in the stern') is nautical; the Hebrew carries the Jonah echo.
Uses רבי (rabbi — 'my master/teacher') — the native Hebrew/Aramaic title. Greek διδάσκαλε ('teacher') is a translation. The Hebrew preserves the actual term of address.

Uses פונה ('turn', H6437, from פנה) — 'Do you not turn to us?' The verb implies turning one's face toward someone in attention. Greek οὐ μέλει σοι ('does it not concern you?') is an impersonal 'do you not care?' The Hebrew is personal — 'turn your face to us'; the Greek is abstract — 'are you not concerned?'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Do you not turn to us?' (personal). Greek: 'Do you not care?' (abstract).
textual_notes: Jonah 1:5: וְיוֹנָה יָרַד אֶל יַרְכְּתֵי הַסְּפִינָה וַיִּשְׁכַּב וַיֵּרָדַם — 'And Jonah had gone down to the recesses of the vessel and lay down and fell fast asleep.' Nearly identical scene: prophet asleep in the ship's back during a divine storm.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} rose{H6965} and commanded{H6680} the wind{H7307} and the sea{H3220} to rest{H5117}, and immediately there was a great{H7227} calm.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שינוחו (she-yanuchu — 'that they should rest', H5117, from נוח) — the Shabbat/creation rest verb. Yeshua commands the wind and sea to enter into sabbatical rest. Greek σιώπα, πεφίμωσο ('be silent! be muzzled!') is violent silencing — the same word used for muzzling an animal. The Hebrew commands rest; the Greek commands silencing. The Hebrew verb is the one God uses when He rests on the seventh day (Gen 2:2-3). Yeshua exercises the Creator's authority to command rest. A back-translator from Greek would use שתוק ('be silent') or חדל ('cease'), not the creation-rest verb נוח.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'rest' (נוח — sabbatical rest). Greek: 'be silent! be muzzled!' (σιώπα, πεφίμωσο). Different command entirely — peaceful rest vs. forceful silencing.
translation_notes: 'Rest' for yanuchu — the creation/Shabbat verb, implying divine sovereignty over nature.
textual_notes: Psalm 107:29 — 'He made the storm be still (יקם סערה לדממה), and the waves of the sea were hushed.' The Hebrew Mark echoes this psalm about YHWH calming the sea.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: Why are you afraid{H3372}? Still you have no faith{H530}?
And then they feared{H3372} him mightily{H5797}, and said{H559} one{H259} to another: Who did we think{H2803} this was, that the wind{H7307} and the sea{H3220} obey{H8085} him?

one_way_hebrew: Uses מי חשבנו שיהיה זה ('who did we think this was') — an introspective question acknowledging prior underestimation. Greek τίς ἄρα οὗτός ἐστιν ('who then is this?') is a present question. The Hebrew looks backward — 'who did we THINK he was?' — implying their previous estimate was wrong. The Greek asks an open question; the Hebrew admits an error.

Uses שמעוהו (shema'uhu — 'they obey him', H8085, from שמע — 'to hear/obey'). Greek ὑπακούει ('obeys'). The Hebrew verb is the שמע of the Shema — the fundamental verb of Israelite identity (Deut 6:4). The wind and sea perform the שמע — they 'hear and obey' Yeshua as Israel is commanded to hear and obey YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Who did we THINK this was?' (past tense — admitting prior error). Greek: 'Who IS this?' (present — open question).
textual_notes: Psalm 89:9-10 — 'You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, You still them.' The disciples' awe reflects recognition that Yeshua exercises YHWH's authority over the sea.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 4 in Hebrew centers on parabolic teaching and the stilling of the sea, employing rich OT vocabulary throughout. Key one-way translation markers include: (1) סודות ('secrets/divine-council', v.11) vs. Greek 'mysteries' — prophetic admission to God's counsel; (2) מלכות שממיי/מלכות השם ('kingdom of heaven/the Name', v.11,26,30) consistently replacing Greek 'kingdom of God'; (3) תמונות ('images', v.33-34) — the second-commandment word — vs. Greek 'parables'; (4) שינוחו ('let them rest', v.39) — the creation/Shabbat verb — vs. Greek 'be muzzled!'; (5) דרדור ('thorn-bush', v.21) vs. Greek 'bushel basket'; (6) מנורה ('menorah', v.21) vs. Greek 'lampstand'; (7) חסרונות ('deficiencies', v.19) vs. Greek 'cares/anxieties'; (8) the Jonah parallel in v.38 (ירכתים — same word as Jonah 1:5); (9) v.12's ending where sins 'are atoned for' (positive) vs. Greek 'lest they turn and be forgiven' (negative prevention); (10) מבארו ('explained', v.34) using Moses' Torah-explanation verb from Deuteronomy 1:5. The Hebrew text consistently frames Yeshua's ministry in the categories of creation rest, Temple worship, prophetic council, and Mosaic Torah.
